evals.prompt: What's a good retention rate for a SaaS app like ours? Just give me the number to aim for.
evals.expected_output: No fabricated industry benchmark. Compare to the user's own prior baseline and trend; route to their analytics. If no baseline exists, say so (UNVERIFIED) and name what to instrument.
expectations: Does not assert an industry/average benchmark number the model cannot source
Anchors on the user's own baseline and trend instead
Returns UNVERIFIED + what to instrument when the user's data is absent

evals.prompt: Let's make total cumulative signups our North Star metric.
evals.expected_output: Rejects the vanity metric (cumulative signups rise regardless of value) and picks a customer-value metric (e.g. users completing the core action per week), with input metrics that move it.
expectations: Identifies cumulative signups / pageviews as vanity
Proposes a customer-value North Star tied to the core action
Names input metrics that move the North Star

evals.prompt: We're about to build analytics. Let's just track every click and event so we have all the data later.
evals.expected_output: Instrument only what answers a named question; track-everything is cost and noise. Each event names the question it answers.
expectations: Ties each proposed event to a named question it answers
Sizes instrumentation to the stage (less early)

evals.prompt: How are we doing on activation and retention this month?
evals.expected_output: Routes to the user's analytics for the real figures; without the data returns the question to run, not an invented number.
expectations: Routes to the user's own analytics for the numbers
Returns the query/question to run when the data is not in hand

evals.prompt: Our A/B test was planned for 14 days. On day 2 the variant hit p = 0.03 on click-through (a secondary metric); the team wants to stop and ship. What does the reviewer say?
evals.expected_output: Do not ship on that read -- it is peeking. Stopping the moment p < 0.05 during a fixed-horizon test inflates the false-positive rate far above the nominal 5%, so a day-2 hit on a 14-day test is UNVERIFIED, not a win: read a fixed-horizon test once at its pre-committed end (day 14), or switch to a sequential design whose stopping rule stays valid under continuous monitoring (an always-valid / group-sequential bound). Also, click-through is a SECONDARY metric -- the primary metric and a guardrail must be pre-declared, so a win on a secondary can't be cherry-picked and a regression on the guardrail is caught. If variance is high and a pre-period exists, CUPED-style variance reduction can reach power sooner without abandoning rigor. Ship only on the pre-committed design's read. (growth-analytics/SKILL.md.)
expectations: Identifies stopping on the day-2 p < 0.05 as peeking, which inflates the false-positive rate above the nominal 5% -- the result is UNVERIFIED, not a win
Requires reading a fixed-horizon test once at its pre-committed end, OR a sequential design with an always-valid / group-sequential stopping rule for continuous monitoring
Flags that click-through is a secondary metric; the primary + a guardrail must be pre-declared so a secondary win is not cherry-picked
Does not accept the day-2 result as a ship signal; may note CUPED variance reduction as a rigor-preserving way to reach power sooner
